headline: Study: 73% of Adults Admit Blankets Are Just 'Wearable Rooms'
subheadline: Researchers say the finding has profound implications for architecture and personal space
summary: A new psychology study reveals that most adults conceptualize blankets as portable private spaces rather than mere fabric coverings, with 847 participants reporting 'blanket territories' in shared living situations.
content:
A groundbreaking study from the Hartwell Institute of Behavioral Sciences has confirmed what many have long suspected: the majority of adults view blankets not as simple bedding accessories but as 'wearable rooms' that provide psychological shelter.

The study, which surveyed 2,847 participants across 15 countries, found that 73% of respondents agreed with the statement 'When I am under a blanket, I feel I am in my own private space, separate from the room I am physically in.'

'This completely reframes our understanding of domestic architecture,' said lead researcher Dr. James Chen. 'People aren't just keeping warm. They're constructing temporary personal dwellings. A blanket is functionally a portable studio apartment.'

The research identified several key behaviors supporting the 'wearable room' theory. 84% of participants reported feeling their phone, snacks, and remote control become 'interior furnishings' once brought under a blanket. 67% admitted to feeling 'invaded' when someone lifts their blanket without permission, using language typically associated with home intrusion.

Perhaps most striking: 91% of participants living with partners or roommates reported establishing 'blanket territories' with implicit boundaries, even when sharing a bed or couch.

'My wife and I have separate blankets,' said study participant Derek Morrison of Hartwell Heights. 'We tried sharing one, but it was like trying to share a studio apartment with someone who has completely different thermostat preferences. Now we each have our own wearable rooms and our marriage is stronger.'

The findings have caught the attention of interior designers and architects. Furniture company BLØKK announced it will release a line of 'structured blankets' with internal frames, essentially creating collapsible fabric rooms that can be worn.

'If people want wearable rooms, we'll give them wearable rooms,' said BLØKK creative director Sven Lindqvist. 'Our new Portable Dwelling Collection launches this fall with optional windows.'

Threadit's r/CozyPlaces community has erupted with users sharing photos of elaborate blanket configurations they now proudly call 'my living room within my living room.'

Dr. Chen suggests the implications extend beyond comfort. 'Privacy is increasingly difficult in our connected age. The blanket may be humanity's last truly private architecture. No smart home integration. No cameras. Just fabric and warmth and solitude.'
author: Sarah Mitchell, Lifestyle & Wellness
